chapters.title: Chapter 4: Related Parties and Capital Allocation

lessons.title: Related Party Transactions: The Note Most Investors Skip

body.text: In a related party transaction, the promoter sits on both sides of the table. The note in the annual report tells you how often, how big, and on whose terms.

children.text: In Lesson 6 you saw how group structures create a motive to move value towards entities the promoter owns more of. Related party transactions, or RPTs, are the actual mechanism. When a listed company buys from, sells to, rents from, or lends to a business the promoter controls, the price is set by people who benefit on both sides. Most RPTs are legal, many are sensible, and some are essential. But nearly every serious case of value leakage in Indian markets has run through this one note in the annual report, and most investors scroll straight past it.
Who Counts as a Related Party

Ind AS 24 sets out who must be disclosed, and SEBI's LODR Regulations widen the net for listed companies. Since April 2022, any person or entity in the promoter group is a related party regardless of how much it holds, and so is any shareholder holding 10% or more of the company.

cells: Holding company, subsidiaries, fellow subsidiaries, associates, joint ventures
Directors, CEO, CFO, company secretary, and their close family members
Private companies, LLPs, partnerships, and trusts controlled by promoters, KMP, or their relatives
Any promoter group entity, and any holder of 10% or more of the listed company

body.caption: Common RPT types and what leakage looks like

cells: A group company supplies a specialised input at market price
Paying above market, so the promoter's private company keeps the margin
A group distributor sells in a region the company cannot reach
Selling below market or on very long credit, so profit and cash sit in the promoter's entity
Offices or warehouses leased from the promoter at market rent
Rent well above market, or rising sharply with no change in space
Shared services at cost across a group
Vague 'management' or 'consultancy' fees paid to a promoter entity
Short-term treasury deposits with a well-rated group NBFC at market rates
Inter-corporate deposits or advances to promoter entities that roll over and never come back
Buying a group company's business at an independently valued fair price
Buying promoter assets at inflated prices, or selling company assets to the promoter cheaply

markDefs.definition: A transaction on terms that two unrelated parties, each acting in its own interest, would agree to. The standard every related party transaction is supposed to meet.

children.text: RPTs are not banned. They are approved. The system relies on independent directors and minority shareholders checking that each one is in the ordinary course of business and at
. That is why Lesson 8's question about whether the audit committee is truly independent matters so much here.

body.caption: How RPTs are approved and disclosed in listed companies

cells: Prior approval of all RPTs and material modifications; only independent directors on the committee vote. Omnibus approval for repetitive transactions is allowed, within limits
Approval of specified transactions under Section 188 that are not in the ordinary course of business or not at arm's length
Material RPTs need shareholder approval. Material means above ₹1,000 crore or 10% of annual consolidated turnover, whichever is lower. Related parties cannot vote to approve
Transactions between a listed company's subsidiaries and its related parties are also covered
Detailed RPT disclosures filed with the exchanges every six months, alongside financial results, plus the Ind AS 24 note in the annual report

stats.label: Materiality threshold
stats.context: Of annual consolidated turnover, whichever is lower

stats.label: Who approves material RPTs
stats.context: With related parties barred from voting in favour

body.title: Who Decides?
body.textWithBlank: When a material related party transaction is put to shareholders, the promoter and other related parties are not allowed to ___ in favour of the resolution.
body.explanation: Under LODR Regulation 23, related parties cannot vote to approve material RPT resolutions. That effectively hands the decision to minority shareholders, which is why AGM voting results on RPT resolutions are so informative.

children.text: Reading the Note: A Worked Example

The raw RPT note is a long list of names and numbers. On its own it tells you almost nothing. The skill is converting it into ratios and trends. Here is an illustrative extract for a fictional listed packaged foods company, with its revenue and net worth for context.

body.latex: \text{RPT Receivable Days} = \frac{\text{Receivable from Related Party}}{\text{Annual Sales to Related Party}} \times 365 \qquad \text{RPT Exposure} = \frac{\text{RPT Receivables} + \text{RPT Loans and Deposits}}{\text{Net Worth}}
body.caption: Two ratios that turn the RPT note into a risk measure
The same note, converted into ratios

cells: Sales to related distributor as % of revenue
RPT exposure as % of net worth

body.title: Related party flows and balances (₹ crore)

children.text: Read what the ratios say. Revenue grew about 11.8% a year, but sales to the promoter-linked distributor grew about 59% a year and now make up nearly a quarter of revenue. That distributor pays in 150 days and slowing. Warehouse rent to the promoter tripled in one year. A deposit to a promoter realty company appeared from nothing. Together, 39% of the company's net worth is now owed by promoter-linked entities. Any one line could have an explanation. The combined pattern says the company's growth is increasingly booked with the promoter's own businesses, and the cash is increasingly sitting with them too.

body.title: Calculate the Receivable Days
body.prompt: In FY26, the company sold ₹610 crore of goods to Prime Distributors LLP, and ₹250 crore was still receivable from it at year end. How many days of sales does that receivable represent? Round to the nearest whole day.
body.explanation: ₹250 crore ÷ ₹610 crore × 365 = 149.6, or about 150 days. If the company's other customers pay in around 45 days, the related distributor is enjoying more than three times the normal credit period. That is a quiet way of lending the company's working capital to a promoter entity, without it ever appearing as a loan.

body.text: Growth booked through related parties deserves a discount, not a premium. If a rising share of revenue comes from a promoter-linked distributor that pays slowly, reported sales and profits may be real on paper while the cash never fully arrives. Always check operating cash flow against profit in companies with large RPT sales.

body.caption: You rarely see the prices, so test the pattern

cells: RPT purchases as % of total purchases and RPT sales as % of revenue, and how both have moved over five years
Whether gross margin falls as RPT purchases rise, or as RPT sales rise, which hints at unfavourable pricing
Receivable days on related parties versus the company's overall receivable days
Whether the related party does something the company could not easily get from an independent supplier or distributor
Whether material RPTs were put to shareholders, how public institutions voted, and whether the audit committee cited independent pricing or valuation

children.text: Maruti Suzuki and the Gujarat Plant: Letting Minorities Decide

In 2014, Maruti Suzuki announced that a new plant in Gujarat would be owned by its Japanese parent, Suzuki Motor Corporation, and would manufacture cars exclusively for Maruti. Institutional investors objected strongly: a large share of Maruti's future production would be controlled by the promoter rather than the listed company. After the backlash, the contract was revised to supply vehicles at cost with no profit to Suzuki's subsidiary, and the arrangement was put to a shareholder vote in which Suzuki did not vote, so minority shareholders made the call. They approved it. The lesson is not that the deal was good or bad. It is that a very large RPT was restructured and decided by the shareholders it affected, before the stricter LODR rules made that the norm.
Fortis Healthcare: When Deposits Went to Promoter Entities

In 2017 and 2018, it emerged that funds from Fortis Healthcare had been placed as short-term deposits that ended up with entities linked to its then promoters, Malvinder and Shivinder Singh. The auditor raised concerns before signing results, an internal investigation followed, and in October 2018 SEBI ordered the former promoters and related entities to repay about ₹403 crore to Fortis. What looked like routine treasury deposits in the accounts had become a route for cash to leave the listed company.

columns.label: Generally Comfortable
points: RPTs small relative to revenue and net worth, and stable over time
Mostly transactions with wholly owned subsidiaries that consolidate into your numbers
Normal credit terms and no loans to promoter entities
Large RPTs put to a vote with strong public institutional support
Clear business rationale explained in the annual report or AGM notice

columns.label: Red Flags
points: Share of revenue or purchases through promoter entities rising year after year
Related parties paying far slower than other customers
Loans, deposits, or advances to promoter entities that roll over or grow
New related parties appearing with no explanation
Omnibus approvals sought for amounts far above historical transactions

body.title: Which RPT Worries You Most?
body.question: All four transactions below are disclosed in a listed company's RPT note and were approved by the audit committee. Which should concern a minority shareholder the most?
options: ₹12 crore of IT services bought from a wholly owned subsidiary at cost
₹2 crore of office rent paid to the promoter, unchanged for five years and in line with nearby commercial rents
₹180 crore of inter-corporate deposits to a promoter-owned real estate company, rolled over for the third year with interest accrued but not received
Dividend of ₹40 crore paid to the promoter holding company along with all other shareholders
body.explanation: Transactions with wholly owned subsidiaries consolidate back into your numbers, stable market rent is benign, and a dividend paid equally to all shareholders is not leakage. A deposit to a promoter-owned business outside the listed group, rolled over repeatedly with interest accruing but not being paid, is the classic pattern of cash that may never come back.

body.title: The Omnibus Approval
body.scenario: A mid cap specialty chemicals company's AGM notice seeks shareholder approval for related party transactions with Apex Petrochem Pvt Ltd, a company owned by the promoter family, of up to ₹1,500 crore a year for three years, covering purchase of raw materials and sale of intermediates. Last year's actual transactions with Apex were ₹310 crore. The company's revenue is ₹4,200 crore. The explanatory statement says the transactions are 'in the ordinary course of business and at arm's length' but gives no pricing basis or independent benchmark. A proxy advisor has recommended voting against.
body.prompt: How should a minority shareholder vote, and why? What information would change your view?
body.modelAnswer: Vote against as proposed. The requested limit of ₹1,500 crore is nearly five times last year's ₹310 crore and about 36% of revenue, so the approval would let a large share of the company's business run through a promoter-owned company for three years without coming back to shareholders. The explanatory statement asserts arm's length pricing without evidence. Because this is a material RPT, the promoter cannot vote in favour, so minority votes decide the outcome, which is exactly when voting matters. You would reconsider if the company reduced the limit close to realistic expected volumes, disclosed the pricing mechanism, such as a link to published petrochemical benchmarks, provided an independent third-party pricing or transfer pricing opinion, explained why Apex rather than independent suppliers, and shortened the approval period to one year so shareholders can review actual transactions.

body.title: Read the RPT Note of One of Your Holdings
steps: Open the latest annual report from screener.in's Documents section and find the related party disclosures note in the consolidated and standalone financial statements
Separate transactions with wholly owned subsidiaries from transactions with promoter-owned or promoter-linked entities outside the listed group
For the promoter-linked entities, calculate RPT sales as % of revenue, RPT purchases as % of total purchases, and RPT receivables plus loans as % of net worth
Repeat for the previous two years' annual reports to see the trend
Calculate receivable days on related parties and compare with the company's overall receivable days
Check the latest half-yearly RPT disclosure on BSE or NSE for any new related parties or large new balances
Search the last three AGM notices for material RPT resolutions and read the public institutional voting results

body.text: Companies and individuals named in this lesson are discussed based on public disclosures, regulatory orders, and widely reported events, for education only. The worked example uses fictional companies. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

points: Related party transactions are the main mechanism through which value moves from a listed company to promoter-controlled entities

Since 2022, all promoter group entities and holders of 10% or more are related parties, and material RPTs above ₹1,000 crore or 10% of consolidated turnover, whichever is lower, need shareholder approval with related parties barred from voting in favour
The raw note means little until converted into ratios: RPT share of revenue and purchases, RPT receivable days, and RPT exposure as a percentage of net worth
In the worked example, related party sales grew about 59% a year against revenue growth of about 11.8%, and promoter-linked entities owed 39% of net worth
Prices are rarely disclosed, so test arm's length through share, margins, credit terms, necessity, and shareholder scrutiny
Large RPTs decided by minority shareholders, as at Maruti Suzuki, are a sign of good process; deposits flowing to promoter entities, as at Fortis Healthcare, are the danger case
